criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Identifies three issues with significance, links to design trade-off, shows organisational context of calendar-driven testing and conflict of interest, plus detailed 6-stakeholder table with interests and decisions.

evidence.quote: Engineering design always trades quality against cost and time
Whether to give quality sign-off; whether to escalate

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Objective for and against arguments with depth, qualifications and rebuttals, leading to differentiated recommendations for Rachel, management, health department, supplier and product engineers.

evidence.quote: Shipping on time protects a real competitive advantage.
The strongest objection is harm to people who have no say.
Rachel should withhold quality sign-off for the health contract

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: Logical flow from for/against to risk-based decision rule to options comparison to justified conclusion. Shows systematic understanding of risk transfer to non-consenting patients versus informed stakeholders.

evidence.where: How should Rachel decide when to ship?
evidence.quote: Neither never ship a defect nor ship unless someone could be physically hurt
Shipping on the current basis is therefore not an ethical way to conduct business.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Well substantiated with 8 reputable sources and both quantitative data and qualitative analysis. Acknowledges limits of analogies, demonstrating balanced in-depth understanding.

evidence.quote: took a charge of US$475 million

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections serving their functions (abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion); maps, figures, tables, and visual elements are correctly used to support discussion; writing is grammatically correct, fluent, concise, easy to read and understand, and uses appropriate word choice; references are well-structured and appropriate, supporting the report’s motivations.
criteria.reasoning: Has abstract, introduction, body, conclusion plus recommendations. Fluent concise writing, competent Table 1, Table 2 and Figure 1 decision flowchart, consistent IEEE references extensively used.

evidence.quote: Table 1: Stakeholders, their interests and the decision each controls.
Engineers Australia, Code of Ethics and Guidelines on Professional Conduct.

overall: Exemplary ethics report meeting all brief requirements with balanced evidence-based argument, clear risk-based shipping rule and stakeholder-specific recommendations.

feedback.summary: You produced an exemplary report meeting all brief requirements. Your balanced for/against analysis, risk-based shipping rule and stakeholder-specific recommendations were strong, supported by quantitative evidence and clear visuals. You achieved Excellent in all criteria – maintain this standard.
next_steps: Continue using your risk-based shipping rule and Table 2 options comparison to justify recommendations in future ethics analyses.
Keep supporting each claim with both quantitative data and qualitative sources as you did with the 19,000 cancellations and $475m charge.
Maintain your use of stakeholder tables and Figure 1 flowchart to make complex decisions clear for readers.
